senses.gloss:
Jyā is the regular word for ‘bowstring’ in the Rigveda and later. The making of bowstrings was a special craft, as is shown by the occurrence of the jyā-kāra, or ‘maker of bowstrings,’ among the victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice, in the yajurveda. The bowstring consisted of a thong of ox-hide. It was not usually kept taut, but was specially tightened when the bow was to be used. The sound of the bowstring (jyā-ghoṣa) is referred to in the Atharvaveda.
Cf. ārtnī.

Jyākā means ‘bowstring,’ with a contemptuous sense, in the Rigveda, and in the simple sense in the Atharvaveda.
Foot notes x. 133, 1, where anyakeṣāṃ jyākāḥ is unmistakably contemptuous. Cf. Macdonell, Vedic Grammar, p. 137.
i. 2, 2.

Jyā-hroḍa occurs in the description of the arms of the vrātya in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa, and is also mentioned in the Sūtras. The sense is somewhat obscure, for one sūtra describes it as a ‘bow not meant for use’ (ayogyaṃ dhanus), while the other speaks of it as a ‘bow without an arrow’ (dhanuṣka aniṣu). Some sort of a bow, therefore, seems to be meant.
